t.1.65.1: Then the mighty-armed one, having dismissed those ministers, went on alone, but he did not see in that hermitage the seer of rigorous vows.
t.1.65.2: Not seeing the seer, and finding the hermitage empty, he called out loudly, "Who is here?", as if making the forest resound.
t.1.65.3: Then, hearing that call of his, a maiden like Śrī in bodily form came out of that hermitage, wearing the garb of a female ascetic.
t.1.65.4: As soon as the dark-eyed maiden saw King Duḥṣanta, she quickly honored him in return and said, "Welcome to you!"
t.1.65.5: Having honored him with a seat, with water for his feet and with the guest-offering, she asked the lord of men, O king, about his health and well-being.
t.1.65.6: Having duly honored him and then asked after his health, she said, as if smiling, "What is to be done? Let it be done."
t.1.65.7: Then the king, duly honored, having seen the sweet-spoken maiden whose every limb was flawless, spoke to her.
t.1.65.8: I have come to pay homage to the illustrious seer Kaṇva. Where has the blessed one gone, good lady? Tell me that, O lovely one.
t.1.65.9: My father, the blessed one, has gone from the hermitage to gather fruits. Wait just a moment, and you will see him when he has come back here.
t.1.65.10: Not seeing the seer, and having been addressed thus by her, the king, beholding that radiant maiden of lovely hips and charming smile,
t.1.65.11: To her, radiant with beauty, with austerity and with self-restraint, endowed with loveliness and youth, the lord of the earth spoke thus.
t.1.65.12: Who are you, and whose are you, O lady of lovely hips, and for what purpose have you come to the forest? Endowed with such beauty and virtues, from where do you come, O radiant one?
t.1.65.13: For by the mere sight of you, O lovely one, my heart has been stolen away by you. I wish to know you, so tell me that, O beautiful one.
t.1.65.14: Thus addressed then by that king in the hermitage, the maiden, laughing, spoke these words of very sweet syllables.
t.1.65.15: O Duḥṣanta, I am known as the daughter of the blessed Kaṇva, the ascetic, steadfast, renowned knower of dharma.
t.1.65.17: How did you, O lady of excellent complexion, come to be born as his daughter? Great is my doubt about this; you should dispel it for me here.
t.1.65.16: The blessed lord, greatly fortunate and honored by the world, is one who has drawn his seed upward in perfect chastity. Dharma itself might swerve from its course, but he of rigorous vows would never swerve.
t.1.65.18: Hear, O king, truly how this origin of mine came about, how this happened long ago, and how I am the daughter of the sage.
t.1.65.20: Long ago, it is said, Viśvāmitra, practicing great austerity, sorely tormented Śakra, the lord of the hosts of the gods.
t.1.65.19: A certain seer came here and asked about my birth; hear, O king, how the blessed one told it to him.
t.1.65.21: "This one, whose power blazes through his austerity, might cast me down from my place," thus fearing, Puraṃdara therefore spoke these words to Menakā.
t.1.65.23: That Viśvāmitra, of great austerity and resplendent like the sun, practising terrible austerities, makes my mind tremble.
t.1.65.22: Menakā, you excel among the Apsarases in divine qualities. Do what is good for me, lovely one; hear what I shall tell you.
t.1.65.24: Menakā, this Viśvāmitra is your burden, O slender-waisted one; of rigorous self-discipline and very hard to assail, he is engaged in fierce austerity.
t.1.65.25: So that he may not topple me from my position, go to him and tempt him. Go, make an obstacle to his austerities, and do me this highest favor.
t.1.65.26: O lovely-hipped one, entice him with your beauty, youth, sweetness, gestures, smiles and words, and turn him back from his austerity.
t.1.65.28: When even you are afraid of the brilliance, the austerity and the wrath of that great-souled one, how should I not be afraid?
t.1.65.27: That blessed one is of great splendor, ever of great austerity, and quick to anger as well; indeed, your lordship too knows him to be so.
t.1.65.29: He who deprived the illustrious Vasiṣṭha of his beloved sons, and who, though first born among the Kṣatriyas, became a Brāhmaṇa by sheer force of will.
t.1.65.30: He who, for the sake of purification, made a river hard to cross with its many waters, the one that people in the world know as the most holy Kauśikī.
t.1.65.31: It was there that long ago, in a time of hardship, the righteous royal sage Mataṅga, who had become a hunter, supported the wife of that great-souled one.
t.1.65.32: When the time of famine had passed, the mighty sage, having come back again to his hermitage there, then gave the river the name Pārā.
t.1.65.33: There he himself, with a gladdened mind, performed a sacrifice on behalf of Mataṅga, and out of fear of him you, O lord of heroes, went there to drink the Soma.
t.1.65.35: He whose deeds are these, of him I am greatly afraid; command me, O lord, in such a way that he, enraged, may not burn me.
t.1.65.34: He who, enraged, outdid the lineages of the stars with a wealth of constellations of his own, and created in rivalry a new set of constellations beginning with Śravaṇa.
t.1.65.37: How could a girl such as I touch one like him, endowed with austerity, blazing like a fire, his senses conquered?
t.1.65.39: Yama and Soma and the great seers, the Sādhyas, the Viśvas, and all the Vālakhilyas, even these tremble before his power; why then should one such as I not tremble before him?
t.1.65.36: With his fiery power he could burn up the worlds and shake the earth with his foot; he could compress the great Meru and swiftly whirl it around as well.
t.1.65.38: O best of the gods, how could one such as I touch that blazing one whose mouth is the fire, whose eyes are the sun and the moon, and whose tongue is Time itself?
t.1.65.40: And having been told thus by you, how could I not go near the ṛṣi, O lord of the gods? But think of protection for me, O king of the gods, so that, protected, I may move about for your sake.
t.1.65.41: But, O god, let Māruta lay bare my garment there as I play, and by your grace, O lord of the gods, may Manmatha become my helper in that task.
t.1.65.42: "And let a fragrant wind blow from the forest at that time, while I am seducing that seer." When he had said "So be it" and that had been arranged, she then went to the hermitage of Kauśika.
